snippet.title: You See a Kangaroo Stuck in a Lake. Survive the Kangaroo.
snippet.description:
A kangaroo standing chest-deep in a lake in Australia looks stuck. It isn't. Don't go in to help it.

Fact-checked. Kangaroos flee into water when a predator such as a dingo or a dog chases them, and a big male can hold a dog under and drown it (Graeme Coulson, University of Melbourne; Live Science). Red kangaroo males stand up to about 1.8 m tall and weigh up to around 90 kg; they hop at more than 50 km/h and can cover 8-9 m in a single bound (San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance; Australian Museum). Standing upright and rubbing the chest are male dominance displays, and fighting males lean back on the tail to kick with both hind feet (Queensland Government).

Queensland Government advice if an aggressive kangaroo approaches: don't turn your back or run; give a short, deep cough, avoid eye contact, bow your head and keep your arms close as you move away slowly; hold any object you have out in front of you as a barrier, and get a tree or a fence between you. Among kangaroos, a lower-ranking male acknowledges a dominant one with a short cough.

When a kangaroo walks slowly it uses its tail as a fifth leg; the tail delivers more propulsive force than the front and hind legs combined (O'Connor et al. 2014, Biology Letters). Never feed kangaroos: fed animals learn to approach people and can turn aggressive (Queensland Government).

Music: "Gonna Fly Now" (theme from "Rocky", Bill Conti), short excerpt.

This is general information, not professional advice.
